newsitem.title: FRANCE: Freed FIS chief vows to seek end to Algeria violence.
newsitem.headline: Freed FIS chief vows to seek end to Algeria violence.

text.p: Algeria's radical Islamist leader Abassi Madani said on Thursday he and his supporters would do all they could to end the violence that had shaken Algeria for more than five years.
Speaking to a correspondent as he headed from an Algiers mosque to his mother's home in Belcourt, central Algiers, the leader of the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) said:
"We are going to do all we can to end this situation."

Madani was suddenly freed from prison last Tuesday, halfway through a 12-year sentence imposed in 1992 for threatening the security of the North African state. Algerian newspapers say he has always refused up to now to renounce or condemn violence.
The FIS leadership in exile said his release contributed to solving the crisis, but diplomats question how much influence he now has and what his release might do.

"...it is not going to stop the violence like the bomb in Baraki yesterday or the massacres," one diplomat said just after Madani's release. "There's no reason to think that Madani can do that now. His time has gone by."
Asked about his making an appeal for calm, the bearded 66-year-old leader said on Thursday: "I can do nothing for the moment since I am not informed on the situation which currently exists.
"I don't want my appeal to be launched into the void."

The country of 29 million people has changed vastly since he was arrested. The FIS was then the most powerful opposition voice in the land and went on to dominate Algeria's first multi-party general election which was scrapped in January 1992.
Now his party is outlawed, its grip on mosques and townhalls broken, and many of its most active militants either in jail, dead or operating underground.
Any leadership claims it might have to a guerrilla movement are more than challenged by the Armed Islamic Group (GIA).

Madani, who has already held meeting with some former senior members of the outlawed party, said: "We should now launch the bomb of life after the bomb of death has been launched at us in our country."
And he added: "My intentions are all good for Algeria."

The FIS leader was walking the 200 metres (yards) home from the Belcourt mosque, dubbed the "Kabul" mosque after the so-called "Afghans" who used it. They were fundamentalist Algerian radicals who had either fought or trained in Afghanistan before Soviet troops pulled out.

Madani said he was in good health but was a bit tired "because of some 15 years of prison that my body has suffered. It must be 15 years if you take account of all the periods I spent in prison, from the time of (former colonial master) France and after. For an individual, that's a lot."
He insisted that his release was "only justice".
"As my detention was an injustice, my liberation should not constitute a great event," he commented.
As he walked, children and adults surrounded him, some asking him about his deputy Ali Belhadj, still detained.
Belhadj was tried alongside Madani in Blida military court in 1992 and also received a 12-year jail sentence.
"I hope that he will be freed soon," said Madani, adding: "At the start we were together in prison, then after I was isolated."
On Wednesday, the newspaper Liberte said Belhadj would soon appear in court over a letter which he sent from prison in 1995 to the then leader of the GIA, Cherif Gousmi.
The authorities have said the letter urged guerrillas to step up attacks and was found on Gousmi's body after the rebel leader was shot and killed by security forces.
Responding to a question about massacres of civilians, blamed by the authorities on fundamentalist rebels, Madani said, without amplifying: "Don't tell me it is the sheep that kill the wolves".
Just one day before Madani was freed, a bomb ripped through an Algiers market. Officials said it killed 21 people and wounded 40.
That attack followed a weekend of massacres and kidnappings in villages in which 44 people died, including 14 women and four adolescents, according to Algerian newspapers.
About 60,000 people have been killed in the conflict since 1992 and staunch republicans in Algeria questioned the wisdom of freeing Madani.
"The Islamists of the FIS are fanatics who consider any measure of mercy a sign of weakness," said El Watan newspaper.
And Liberte said Madani had already given "a very virulent speech against the authorities" to some of his visitors.
